summary: This unit is about behaving professionally and ethically at work, in any trade. You will learn what professionalism, ethics and integrity mean, and how they show in punctuality, appearance, honesty, confidentiality, fair dealing with customers and working within your competence. You will also learn how to handle gifts, bribes and conflicts of interest, how to report wrongdoing and own your mistakes, and how to keep your skills up to date.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423), and the same unit is taken by trainees in other trades, such as electrical installation and cosmetology. It is about **how you behave at work**: being reliable, honest, respectful and safe, so that customers, employers and co-workers can trust you.

Skill alone does not keep a tradesperson in work. A welder who overcharges, an electrician who signs for tests he did not do, or a stylist who gossips about clients soon loses customers, and in a small community the story spreads fast. A trainee who is punctual, honest and careful gets good references, steady work and, later, a business of their own.

**Who it is for:** trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, in any trade. The examples come from welding, electrical installation and the salon, but the same rules apply in every workplace.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Explain professionalism and ethics
Say what professionalism, ethics, integrity and a work ethic mean, and why they matter to you, customers and the business.
Keep good attendance and appearance
Arrive on time and ready, report lateness and sickness properly, follow the dress code and keep good personal hygiene.
Act honestly
Deal honestly with money, materials, time and records, and use the employer's property only with permission.
Handle gifts and conflicts of interest
Recognise a bribe, refuse it politely, and declare anything that could affect a decision you make for work.
Keep information confidential
Protect customers' and the business's private information, at work and on social media.
Work within your competence
Do only the work you are trained, qualified and allowed to do, refuse unsafe instructions, and keep your skills up to date.
Deal fairly with customers
Give clear prices and receipts, keep promises, respect people's property, treat everyone fairly and handle complaints calmly.
Follow rules and report problems
Follow the contract, policies and code of conduct, report wrongdoing properly, and own your mistakes.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on professionalism, ethics, attendance, appearance, honesty, confidentiality, competence, gifts and conflicts of interest, conduct, fair dealing and reporting.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact words such as punctuality, bribe, whistle-blower, dress code, CPD, reputation) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** in a group: writing a code of conduct for a work area and deciding what to do in ethics case cards; then a role play of one customer's job from first visit to complaint, including an honest quotation, a delay, refusing a side deal and handling a complaint.

blocks.note: Many questions describe a situation and ask what a professional would do. Look for the answer that is honest, legal, safe and fair to everyone, and that brings in the supervisor when the decision is not yours to make.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Professionalism** means behaving at work in a skilled, reliable, honest and respectful way, so that people can trust you. It is not about expensive clothes, or how many years you have been in the trade. A trainee in their first week can be more professional than someone with twenty years' experience.

**Ethics** means knowing what is right and fair, and doing it. Your **values** are the beliefs you hold about what is right and important, such as honesty, respect, fairness and responsibility. **Integrity** means sticking to those values and doing right even when nobody is watching.

head: Term
What it means
Example at work
rows: Professionalism
Skilled, reliable, honest and respectful behaviour at work
Arriving on time, in clean PPE, and doing the job to the standard agreed
Ethics
Knowing and doing what is right and fair
Charging a tourist the same fair price as a local customer
Integrity
Being honest and doing right even when no one is watching
Recording the real time you started work, though nobody would check
Work ethic
Working hard and doing a good job without being watched
Carrying on cleaning welds properly while the supervisor is out
Accountability
Accepting responsibility for your work and its results
Owning up to a mistake and helping to put it right
Reputation
The good or bad name a worker or business has with the public
Customers recommending a stylist to their friends
Courtesy
Politeness and good manners towards everyone
Greeting a customer by name and thanking them
Fairness
Treating everyone equally, without favourites
Serving customers in the order they arrived

head: For you
For customers
For the business
rows: You keep your job and get good references
You are trusted with better work and promotion
You build a name you can later take into your own business
They are safe, and get the work they paid for
They are treated with respect and get value for money
They can trust you in their home, with their money and with their information
Customers come back and recommend it
Fewer complaints, disputes and legal problems
Its name in the community stays good

blocks.note: Most small trades in Jamaica live on **word of mouth**. The gate man, the electrician or the stylist in a community gets most of their work because someone recommended them. One story of overcharging, theft or a careless job travels quickly, now on WhatsApp and social media too, and is hard to undo.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: When you are not sure whether something is right, ask yourself these questions in turn:

flow: Is it legal?
Does it follow the workplace's rules and code of conduct?
Is it honest and fair to everyone: the customer, the employer and your co-workers?
Is it safe?
Would I be happy for my supervisor, the customer and my family to know about it?
If any answer is "no" or "not sure": do not do it; ask your supervisor

blocks.p: Put simply, a professional worker is **punctual, honest, skilled, polite and safe**. They also keep their work area tidy, keep learning, and can be trusted to do what they say they will do.

**Punctuality** means arriving on time and keeping to agreed times. "On time" means **ready to start** at the start time: changed, PPE on and tools out. So arrive a few minutes early. If your supervisor asks you to arrive 15 minutes before a 7:30 a.m. start, you arrive by 7:15 a.m.

ul: Plan for the delays you know about: traffic, a full route taxi, rain, a bus that does not come. Leave home early enough to cover them.

If you will be late or absent, **call your supervisor before the shift starts**, explain, and say when you expect to arrive. Do not just turn up late and explain afterwards, and do not stay away without a word.
Never ask a co-worker to sign you in, or to cover for you with a story. That is dishonest for both of you.
Keep to your agreed break and lunch times, and come back on time.
**Absenteeism** means staying away from work often without good reason. It quickly loses you the employer's trust.

head: Who is affected by lateness and absence
How
rows: The team
Others must cover your work, under more pressure and for longer hours. Team tasks, such as lifting a heavy gate, may be done short-handed and unsafely. Bad feeling grows.
Customers
Jobs start late, appointments are moved or cancelled, promises are broken, and customers go elsewhere.
The business
Work is not finished, overtime may have to be paid, and the business's reputation suffers.
You
Warnings, lost pay, no promotion and, in the end, losing the job. Good attendance is often a reason for promotion.

ul: Tell your supervisor as early as you can, and follow the workplace's sick-leave rules, such as bringing a doctor's certificate when the rules ask for one.
Do not come in with a fever, a bad cough or a stomach bug to work closely with clients or co-workers: you spread the illness.
Do not simply stay home without telling anyone. Your supervisor needs to plan the work.

blocks.p: Your appearance tells a customer, before you say a word, whether you take your work seriously. Follow the **dress code**: the workplace's rules on what staff wear.

head: Area
What is expected
Why it matters
rows: Body
Bathe daily; use deodorant; fresh breath
You work close to customers and co-workers; body odour gives a poor impression
Uniform or overalls
Clean, in good repair, as the dress code says
Shows respect; customers recognise and trust you
Hair
Neat; tied back or covered where needed
Cannot be caught in a machine or fall on a client
Nails
Short and clean
Stops germs spreading, especially in beauty and food work
Jewellery
Little or none at work
Rings and chains catch on tools and machines and conduct electricity
Hands
Washed before and after each client or job, and after the toilet
Stops the spread of germs
PPE
The right PPE for the task, clean and in good repair
Protects you; shows you work safely

head: Trade
Professional appearance includes
rows: Welding and fabrication
Cotton or flame-resistant overalls, no polyester or nylon (they melt)
Leather safety boots; no rings or chains
Clean, undamaged helmet and gloves
Electrical installation
Clean work clothes and safety boots
No metal watch straps, rings or chains near live parts
Tools and PPE in good order
Cosmetology and beauty
Clean uniform or smock and closed shoes
Hair tied back; short, clean nails
Cuts covered with a waterproof dressing; gloves for chemical work
No strong perfume

blocks.note: Your uniform also speaks for the business outside work. In uniform, or in the company's vehicle, people link what they see you do, how you drive and how you speak to the business's name.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Honesty and integrity: money, time, materials and records

blocks.p: **Honesty** means telling the truth and not stealing, lying or cheating. Customers let tradespeople into their homes and trust them with their money and safety; employers trust workers with tools, materials, vehicles and cash. Honesty is what makes that trust possible.

head: Situation
Dishonest
Honest
rows: A customer pays too much, or you are given too much change
Keep it quietly, or share it with a co-worker
Tell the customer at once and give it back
Offcuts, spare cable, salon products
Take them home because "they will only be thrown away"
They belong to the business: take them only with permission
Work time
Long personal calls, social media, or private jobs during working hours
Use work time for work; personal matters at breaks
Time sheet or attendance register
Write the usual start time after coming in late; sign in for someone else
Write the real times, every time
Bills
Add hours or work that were never done; charge for good parts and fit cheap ones
Charge only for the work done and the materials used
Records
Fill in test results, checks or client records without doing them
Record what was actually done and found
The employer's tools and vehicle
Use them for private jobs without asking
Use them for private work only with the owner's permission

blocks.p: Wasting paid time on personal business is sometimes called **stealing time**. A few minutes a day adds up to hours of work the employer has paid for and not received.

blocks.note: Small amounts still count. "Nobody will miss it" is still stealing, and workers have lost their jobs, and their good name, over a bag of offcuts or a bottle of shampoo.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Other people rely on records to know that work is safe.

ul: An **electrical test sheet** tells the inspector, the customer and the next electrician that the circuits are safe. A false reading can hide a fault that causes a shock or a fire.
A **welding inspection record** or job card tells the customer that the welds were checked.
A **salon client record** shows allergies, skin test results and the products used, so the next stylist can work safely.
A **time sheet** is used to pay you and to bill the customer.

blocks.p: Sign only for work you did and checks you made. Filling in a record without doing the work is dishonest and can be fraud.

ul: Losing your job, and a bad reference that follows you.
Police involvement where there is theft or fraud.
Lost customers and a damaged business.
A bad name in the community, which is very hard to win back.

sections.title: Gifts, bribes and conflicts of interest

blocks.p: A **bribe** is money, a gift or a favour offered to make someone act dishonestly or unfairly: to choose a supplier, pass poor work, skip a queue or look the other way. Offering or taking a bribe is wrong and can be a crime, whatever its value.

head: Situation
Usually acceptable?
What to do
rows: A small thank-you after the job is finished, such as a cake or fruit, shared openly
Usually, if the workplace's rules allow it
Tell your supervisor; share it with the team
A tip from a satisfied client (salon, hotel)
Depends on the workplace's rules
Follow the tipping policy
A gift, cash or favour from a supplier while you are helping to choose a supplier
No
Refuse politely, or report it, as the rules say
"Something for your trouble" to pass work, sign a form or jump the queue
No: it is a bribe
Refuse, and report it to your supervisor
A large or valuable gift from anyone you deal with for work
Usually no
Do not accept it without asking your supervisor

blocks.p: The question to ask is: **could this gift affect a decision I make for work, or make people think it could?** If yes, refuse it.

blocks.note: A polite way to refuse: "Thank you, but our rules don't allow me to accept that. The owner chooses suppliers on price, quality and delivery." Then tell your supervisor about the offer.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **conflict of interest** is when your own gain, or that of your family or friends, could affect a decision you make for work.

ul: Getting prices from a supplier owned by a relative.
Running a side business that competes with your employer, or doing private jobs for your employer's customers.
Recommending a friend for a job, or for a contract, without saying they are your friend.
Using what you know about the business's prices or customers to help yourself or someone else.

flow: Notice the conflict
Tell your supervisor or the owner about it before any decision is made
Step back and let someone else make the decision, if asked
Never pass on the business's private information to help yourself or others

blocks.note: If a customer offers you cash to do a job privately, using the business's tools, materials or time, refuse politely. Explain that the tools and materials belong to the business, offer to book the job properly so the owner can price it, and tell your supervisor about the request. A private side job like this takes business from your employer, is not covered by the business's insurance or guarantee, and puts your job at risk.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Public bodies in Jamaica, such as ministries, agencies and parish councils, have strict rules on gifts and on how contracts are given out. If you work on a government contract, follow those rules exactly.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Confidentiality and conduct at work and online

blocks.p: **Confidentiality** means keeping private information private and using it only for the job. Customers often share information with a worker that could embarrass them, cost them money or even help a thief if it were passed on.

head: Private information
Examples
rows: About customers
Names, phone numbers, addresses, what they paid, when their house is empty, alarm codes and keys, health problems and allergies, personal stories told in the chair
About the business
Prices and costings, supplier prices, customer lists, designs and plans, staff matters

ul: Share information only with staff who need it to do the job.
Do not talk about customers to friends or family, or where others can overhear.
Keep job cards, client record cards and receipts in a safe place, not lying on the counter.
Lock phones and computers that hold customer details.
If you are not sure whether you may share something, for example when someone says the law requires it or a person may be in danger, ask your supervisor.

blocks.note: Jamaica has a data protection law that sets rules for how businesses collect, keep, use and share people's personal information. Your workplace's rules tell you how to handle customer records: follow them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Use your personal phone at breaks, away from customers and work areas. Never use it while operating a machine, or while a client is waiting in the chair.
Do not take photos of customers, their homes or the workplace without permission.
Never post complaints about customers, co-workers or your employer. If a customer was rude, report it at work instead.
Never post anything that shows a customer's address, face, keys, locks or security.
Remember that screenshots last for ever: anything you post can be passed on.

Never come to work under the influence of alcohol, ganja or any other drug. They slow your reactions and judgement and cause accidents with grinders, electricity, chemicals and vehicles. Workplace rules forbid it.
If a medicine makes you drowsy, tell your supervisor before you use machines or drive.
If a co-worker seems drunk or high, do not let them use a machine or tool you are involved with, and tell the supervisor at once.
Speak politely, using the customer's name and language suited to them. No cursing at work.
Use clear Standard English with customers and visitors who need it.
Keep personal problems and arguments away from customers.
Treat the workplace, its tools and its vehicles with care.

sections.title: Working within your competence and keeping up to date

blocks.p: **Competence** means having the knowledge, skill and authority to do a task safely and to the right standard. Do only the work you are trained, qualified and allowed to do. Work done by someone not competent can injure the worker or the customer, damage property, cost money to put right, break the law or the rules of the trade, and may not be covered by the business's insurance.

head: Trade
Examples of work for qualified people only
What a trainee does
rows: Electrical installation
Wiring or rewiring a building alone
Connecting to the supply
Signing test certificates
Works only under a licensed electrician. In Jamaica an installation must be inspected and certified before JPS will connect the supply.
Welding and fabrication
Welding or cutting drums, tanks or cylinders that have held fuel or gas
Load-bearing work such as balcony rails, trailer hitches or structural steel that needs a qualified welder and a procedure
Refers the job to the supervisor; never "tries it"
Cosmetology and beauty
Treating skin infections, rashes or unusual moles
Chemical services without the skin test the maker requires
Treatments you have not been trained in
Advises the client to see a doctor, or refers to a trained colleague

blocks.p: When asked to do work outside your competence: explain politely that it is outside your training, and refer the customer to a qualified person or to your supervisor. Do not "try it anyway", do not do it cheaply "in case it goes wrong", and do not learn it from a video on the spot.

ul: Some trades, such as electrical work, need a **licence** or **certificate** before you may work alone. It shows the worker has been trained and tested to work safely, which protects the public.

NVQ-J certificates, awarded through HEART/NSTA Trust and NCTVET, show you are competent in the units you have passed. Keep your certificates and copies safe; employers and customers may ask to see them.

blocks.p: If you are told to do something unsafe, such as using a cracked grinding disc, a damaged ladder, or working on a live circuit, refuse politely, explain why, and ask for what is needed to do it safely. Then report it. Doing something dangerous because "the supervisor said so" does not make it safe.

blocks.h: Keeping your skills up to date

blocks.p: Methods, tools, materials and rules keep changing: inverter welding machines, LED lighting and solar systems, new hair products and techniques, new safety rules. **CPD (continuing professional development)** means carrying on learning after you qualify.

head: Way to keep learning
Example
rows: Further courses and qualifications
Moving from Level 2 to Level 3 in your trade
Supplier demonstrations
A supplier shows a new welding machine or hair product
Reading instructions
The maker's manual and the safety data sheet for a new product
Learning from experienced workers
Watching, asking questions and asking for feedback on your work
Keeping up with safety rules and standards
New workplace procedures; changes to the standards your trade must meet
Joining a trade group or association
Meeting others and sharing good practice
Setting goals and keeping a training record
A list of courses done and skills gained, with dates

blocks.note: Keep a simple record of every course, demonstration and new skill, with the date. It shows an employer or customer what you can do, and helps you plan what to learn next.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Area
What a professional does
rows: Prices
Gives a clear price, preferably in writing, and explains any extra costs before the work starts. Charges a fair price to everyone, local or visitor.
Materials
Uses the materials the customer paid for. Any change is agreed with the customer first.
Quality
Keeps to the quality standard even when the customer is in a hurry, and agrees a fair time instead of skipping checks.
Promises
Keeps to agreed dates. If a job will be late, contacts the customer early, explains, and gives a new date.
Property
Covers and protects furniture, floors and cars; asks before moving things or using the customer's tools; cleans up afterwards.
Courtesy
Greets the customer, uses their name, speaks politely and keeps personal problems out of the conversation.
Fairness
Serves customers in turn and treats them all with the same respect, whoever they are and whoever they know.
Competitors
Speaks about their own work and does not run down other businesses or tell untrue stories.

ul: Give a **receipt** for every payment: it is the customer's proof that they have paid.
Record every sale as the business requires. Leaving a sale off the books "because the customer does not need a receipt" cheats the business and the tax system, and leaves the customer with no proof.
A business registered for GCT must charge it at the current rate and show it on its bills.

flow: Listen calmly to the whole complaint, without interrupting
Thank the customer for telling you, and say sorry for the trouble
Ask questions to understand exactly what is wrong
Check the work
Explain what will be done and when, or bring in your supervisor if the decision is not yours
Put it right, then check that the customer is satisfied

blocks.note: Never argue, blame the customer, or tell them to leave. Even when the customer is wrong, stay polite and bring in your supervisor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: When you make a mistake on a customer's job

flow: Check how serious it is; if there is any danger, such as a cracked weld, a loose connection or a chemical left on too long, make it safe at once
Tell your supervisor honestly what happened; do not hide it or blame someone else
With your supervisor, tell the customer, say sorry and explain how and when it will be put right
Put it right properly, at no extra cost if the fault was yours
Work out why it happened, so it does not happen again, and record it if the workplace requires

blocks.p: Get rid of used chemicals, oil, paint, solvent, old cable, electrode stubs and salon chemicals the way the maker's safety data sheet and the workplace's rules say. Never pour them into a drain or gully, burn them in the yard, or dump them in the bush. In Jamaica, gullies carry whatever is poured into them to the rivers and the sea.

sections.title: Rules, reporting and owning your work

blocks.h: Your contract, policies and code of conduct

head: Document
What it is
rows: Contract of employment
The agreement you and the employer sign, setting out the job, pay, hours, leave and notice
Policies and procedures
The workplace's rules and set ways of doing things, such as the safety rules, sick-leave procedure and cash-handling procedure. They keep work safe, fair and done to the same standard.
Code of conduct
A written set of rules for how staff should behave

blocks.p: A typical workshop or salon code of conduct covers:

head: Topic
Example rule
rows: Punctuality
Be at your station, changed and ready, by the start time.
Dress and PPE
Wear the uniform and the PPE the task needs, clean and in good repair.
Honesty
Record your real times; take nothing home without permission.
Confidentiality
Do not share customers' details or post about them.
Tools and materials
Use them only for work; return them clean; report damage.
Phones
Personal phones only at breaks, away from machines and clients.
Respect
Speak politely; no bullying, harassment or cursing.
Safety
Follow the safety rules; never bypass a guard.
Reporting
Report faults, injuries, near misses and wrongdoing to the supervisor at once.

blocks.p: If you think a rule is unfair, keep following it, and raise it politely with your supervisor, suggesting a better way. Do not break it, complain to customers, or tell new trainees to ignore it.
Wrongdoing includes theft, cheating customers, falsifying records, unsafe work, bullying and harassment. A worker who reports wrongdoing to someone who can act on it is called a **whistle-blower**.

flow: Do not join in, accept a share, or pretend you did not see it
Do not argue with or threaten the person in public
Write down the facts as soon as you can: what you saw, the date, the time, the place and who else was there
Report it privately to your supervisor, or to the manager or owner if the supervisor is involved, following the workplace's rules
Stick to facts, not rumours, and do not gossip about it
Let the business look into it fairly

blocks.note: Jamaica has a law that protects workers who report serious wrongdoing honestly, through the proper channels. Your workplace's reporting procedure tells you who to go to.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Being **accountable** means accepting responsibility for your work and its results, good or bad.
Fill in your job card, logbook or time sheet truthfully at the end of each job.
Own up to mistakes early, when they are easiest to put right. Blaming the tools, the materials or a co-worker makes things worse.
Finish what you start, or hand it over properly with a clear note of what is left to do.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can explain professionalism, ethics, integrity, work ethic and accountability, with examples.
I can use the ethics check to decide what to do in a difficult situation.
I can explain why punctuality and attendance matter, and what to do if I will be late or sick.
I can describe the appearance, hygiene and PPE expected in my trade, and say why each matters.
I can give examples of honest and dishonest behaviour with money, materials, time and records.
I can recognise a bribe and a conflict of interest, and say how to deal with each.
I can explain confidentiality and keep customers' information private, at work and online.
I can explain why I must work only within my competence, and refuse unsafe instructions politely.
I can describe ways to keep my skills up to date (CPD).
I can deal fairly with customers: clear prices, receipts, kept promises, respect for property.
I can handle a complaint calmly and own a mistake on a customer's job.
I can explain what a contract, policies and a code of conduct are, and write sensible rules.
I can report wrongdoing properly, sticking to the facts.

terms: Staying away from work often without a good reason
Accepting responsibility for your work and its results
Money, a gift or a favour offered to make someone act dishonestly or unfairly
A document showing you have passed a course or are qualified
A written set of rules for how staff should behave
Having the knowledge, skill and authority to do a task safely and well
Keeping private information private and using it only for the job
When your own gain could affect a decision you make for work
The signed agreement that sets out the job, pay and hours
Continuing professional development: carrying on learning after you qualify
The workplace's rules on what staff must wear
Knowing and doing what is right and fair
Keeping your body and clothes clean so that germs do not spread
Being honest and doing right even when no one is watching
Skilled, reliable, honest and respectful behaviour at work
Arriving on time and keeping to agreed times
The document a customer receives to prove they have paid
The good or bad name a worker or business has with the public
The beliefs you hold about what is right and important
A worker who reports wrongdoing to someone who can act on it
Working hard and doing a good job without being watched

c1.title: Ramp handrails at a shop in Linstead
c1.text: Romario, a welding trainee, is on work placement at a small fabrication shop in Linstead, St Catherine. The shop is making handrails for a church's wheelchair ramp from 50 mm round tube with 3 mm walls, as the signed quotation says. On his first morning Romario arrives in a polyester football shirt and canvas sneakers. By Wednesday the 3 mm tube has run out, and the foreman tells him to finish the rails with 2 mm tube from the yard "because the church will never know". That afternoon a co-worker, Fitzroy, comes back from lunch smelling strongly of rum and picks up the angle grinder.

c2.title: Rewiring a house in Santa Cruz
c2.text: Shamar, an electrical installation trainee, is helping a licensed electrician, Mr Grant, rewire an elderly woman's house in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. In the main bedroom, where Shamar must run a cable, there is cash and jewellery on the dresser. The homeowner offers to tell Shamar her bank card PIN "so you can buy more cable if you run short". Later, while Mr Grant is at the hardware store, she asks Shamar to fill in and sign the test sheet for the new wiring so that she can book the inspection sooner.

c3.title: A Saturday at a salon in Half Way Tree
c3.text: Tamika, a cosmetology trainee, works Saturdays at a busy salon in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. A client who has never had colour at this salon wants a permanent hair colour today. The colour maker's instructions and the salon's procedure call for a skin test 48 hours before. The client says, "I have used colour before, just do it." Another client tells Tamika about her divorce while her hair is being washed. Tamika also has a small cut on her finger from cooking at home.

c4.title: Buying square tube in Port Maria
c4.text: Davian is the storekeeper at a fabrication business in Port Maria, St Mary. The owner asks him to get written prices from three suppliers for a large order of square tube. One of the suppliers is owned by Davian's uncle. A sales representative from another supplier tells Davian he will "get a new phone for your trouble" if the order comes to them. The same week, a happy customer brings the whole workshop a cake to say thank you for a finished job.

c5.title: Late arrivals and a new machine in Port Antonio
c5.text: Kemoy is a welder at a marine repair shop in Port Antonio, Portland. This month he has been 20 to 30 minutes late three times, because the route taxi he takes is often full, and his supervisor has spoken to him about it. The shop has also bought a new inverter welding machine with pulse settings that Kemoy has never used. A customer's stainless steel boat rail must be welded on it next week.

questions.q: What should Romario do about his clothes on the first morning?
o: Carry on, since on the first day he will mostly be watching
Change into cotton overalls and safety boots before work
Roll the shirt's sleeves up so that they stay clear of sparks
Wear a welding apron over the shirt and keep the sneakers on
questions.why: Polyester melts onto the skin when a spark lands, and canvas sneakers give no protection from falling steel or hot slag. Following the dress code and wearing the right PPE is part of being professional from day one.

questions.q: What is the professional response to the foreman's instruction about the 2 mm tube?
o: Use the 2 mm tube, because the foreman is in charge of this job
Say politely he is not comfortable, and ask that the owner be told
Use the 2 mm tube, but weld it more heavily to make up for the walls
Refuse loudly in front of the other workers, so everyone knows
questions.why: The church agreed to and paid for 3 mm tube, and a ramp handrail must take people's weight. Swapping it in secret deceives the customer; raise it calmly so the owner and the customer can decide.

questions.q: Fitzroy is about to start the grinder. What should Romario do?
o: Hold the work steady for him so that the cut is safer
Say nothing, as what Fitzroy does at lunch is his business
Tell the other workers to keep well away from Fitzroy's bench
Ask him not to use it, and tell the foreman straight away
questions.why: Alcohol slows reactions and judgement, and a grinder can kick back or burst a disc. A worker who seems impaired must not use machines, and the supervisor must be told at once so they can deal with it.

questions.q: On Thursday Romario misreads his tape and cuts two lengths of tube 100 mm too short. What should he do?
o: Tell the foreman at once, so the pieces can be used elsewhere
Weld short pieces onto the ends so that nobody notices
Put the short pieces in the scrap bin and quietly cut two more
Say that the tape measure must have been faulty
questions.why: Being accountable means owning mistakes. Told early, the foreman can reuse the short pieces and plan the steel; hidden joins weaken a rail, and blaming the tape is dishonest.

questions.q: What should Shamar do about the cash and jewellery?
o: Move them into a drawer himself so they are out of the way
Leave them where they are and work around them without a word
Ask the homeowner to put them away before he works in the room
Put them in his tool bag for safety until the room is finished
questions.why: Asking the owner to secure her valuables protects her property and protects Shamar from any doubt if something goes missing. A worker should not handle a customer's money or jewellery.

questions.q: How should Shamar respond to the offer of the PIN?
o: Write it down and give it to Mr Grant to keep safe
Accept it, and promise to use it only for buying cable
Save it in his phone in case of an emergency
Thank her, refuse, and tell her to keep her PIN private
questions.why: A PIN is private, and knowing it puts both the customer and the worker at risk. Materials are bought through the business, which then bills the customer properly.

questions.q: What should Shamar do about the test sheet?
o: Fill it in with normal readings, so that she can book it sooner
Leave it for Mr Grant, who did the tests and is licensed
Sign Mr Grant's name for him, since he would surely agree to it
Copy the readings from another house they wired last month
questions.why: A test sheet tells the inspector and the customer that the wiring is safe. Only the person who did the tests, and is licensed to, fills it in and signs it; anything else is a false record.

questions.q: What should Tamika do about the permanent colour?
o: Apply the colour today, since the client has used colour before
Use the colour today but leave it on for a shorter time
Explain why, do the skin test today, and book the colour later
Ask the client to sign a note and then go ahead with it today
questions.why: The skin test checks for an allergy that can cause a serious reaction, and the maker's instructions and the salon's procedure require it. Working within procedures protects the client even when she is in a hurry.

questions.q: Later, a friend of the client asks Tamika, "What did she tell you about the divorce?" What should Tamika say?
o: That she does not discuss what clients tell her
Only the main facts, as they are friends anyway
Nothing now, but she will tell her after work
What she knows, as long as nobody else hears
questions.why: What a client says in the chair is confidential. Passing it on breaks her trust and damages the salon's name, even when the person asking is a friend.

questions.q: What should Tamika do about the cut on her finger before she works on clients?
o: Cover it with a waterproof dressing and wear gloves
Leave it uncovered so that it heals faster in the open air
Work as usual on clients, as long as it has stopped bleeding
Wash it with shampoo between clients instead of covering it
questions.why: An open cut lets germs pass between worker and client. A waterproof dressing, gloves and hand washing are part of the hygiene a professional keeps.

questions.q: What should Davian do about his uncle's business?
o: Choose his uncle only if his price is lowest, and say nothing
Leave his uncle's price out so that nobody can complain
Tell the owner about the family link before any choice is made
Tell his uncle the lowest price so that his uncle can beat it
questions.why: A family link is a conflict of interest: his own interest could affect a decision he makes for work. Declaring it lets the owner decide fairly; passing on other suppliers' prices would be dishonest.

questions.q: What makes the phone offer wrong, when the cake is acceptable?
o: It is worth more money than the cake the customer brought
It is offered to sway a decision Davian is making for work
It is offered to one person, while the cake is for everyone
It comes from a supplier, and suppliers' gifts are always bribes
questions.why: A bribe is anything offered to make someone act unfairly, whatever its value. The cake is a small thank-you after the job, shared openly, and cannot change any decision; the phone is meant to buy the order.

questions.q: Is it acceptable for the workshop to accept the customer's cake?
o: No: workers may never accept anything at all from a customer
Yes, but only the foreman should keep it, since he led that job
No: it must be sent back politely with a note thanking the customer
Yes: a small thank-you shared openly after a job is usually fine
questions.why: Small, openly shared thank-you gifts after the work is done do not influence decisions and are usually allowed. Check the workplace's rules and tell the supervisor; cash or valuable gifts are a different matter.

questions.q: A friend who works at a rival shop asks Davian what price per length he was given for the tube. What should he say?
o: The price, since prices are much the same everywhere
That supplier prices are private to the business
The price, if the friend promises to tell nobody
A higher price, so that the rival shop pays more
questions.why: Prices and costings are the business's confidential information; passing them on can help a competitor undercut it. Lying is not the answer either: simply decline politely.

questions.q: What is the professional way for Kemoy to deal with his lateness?
o: Leave home earlier or find other transport, so he is on time
Explain each time that the taxi was full, as it is not his fault
Ask a co-worker to tell the supervisor he is already on site
Stay back after work, without asking, to make up the time
questions.why: Punctuality means planning for delays you know about. Excuses do not get the work started, cover stories are dishonest, and extra hours must be agreed with the supervisor, not simply taken.

questions.q: How should Kemoy prepare to use the new machine on the customer's rail?
o: Try out settings on the customer's rail until the weld looks right
Set the highest pulse setting, since that gives the strongest weld
Use it without the pulse, and ask for help only if something fails
Read the maker's manual and practise on scrap with guidance first
questions.why: New equipment means new learning. Reading the manual and practising on scrap under guidance is part of keeping your skills up to date; the customer's job is not the place to experiment.

questions.q: A welder wants to post photos of a finished set of burglar bars on the business's page. Which is the professional approach?
o: Post the photos at once, since the work belongs to the welder who did it
Post them with the street name, so that neighbours can call for work
Get permission, and show nothing that identifies the house or its security
Post them only on a personal page, where the workplace's rules do not apply
questions.why: Photos of a customer's home can show where they live and how their security works. Ask the employer and the customer first, and keep addresses, faces and locks out of the picture.

questions.q: Which is the most professional way to answer the workshop or salon phone?
o: Say "Yes?" and wait for the caller to explain why they are calling
Answer while finishing a chat with a co-worker, to save time
Greet the caller, name the business and yourself, and offer help
Ask the caller to ring back later, when someone senior is in
questions.why: First impressions on the phone count. A clear greeting with the business name and your own name tells callers they have the right place and will be dealt with politely.

questions.q: You are unsure whether something you have been asked to do at work is ethical. Which question is the best test?
o: Would I be happy for my supervisor, customer and family to know?
Will anyone find out about it if I do it quietly and say nothing?
Will I earn more money from it this week than I would otherwise?
Is everyone else in the trade already doing the same thing anyway?
questions.why: If you would want to hide it, it is probably wrong. Check that it is legal, within the rules, honest, fair and safe; if you are still unsure, ask your supervisor before you act.

questions.q: Two customers are waiting at the counter. The second to arrive is your cousin. Who should you serve first?
o: Your cousin first, because family comes first
Whichever of the two looks ready to spend more
Your cousin first, as long as it is done quickly
The customer who arrived first, then your cousin
questions.why: Fairness means treating every customer the same way. Serving people in turn shows customers they can trust the business, whoever they are and whoever they know.
